planting.note: Sow onto bare, sandy soil in fall so seedlings can establish a basal rosette over winter before flowering the following summer.

directions: Sow onto bare, sandy soil in fall so seedlings can establish a basal rosette over winter before sending up soft, gray-green hairy stems topped with classic yellow, dark-centered coneflowers the following summer. Native to the Florida Panhandle, southern Georgia, and Alabama sandhills and pine flatwoods, it is well suited to the dry, well-drained sandy soils found across the Gulf Coastal Plain. Its blooms attract a wide range of native bees, butterflies, and beneficial wasps, and the seed heads feed goldfinches into fall and winter. Give it full sun and lean soil, since rich, moist conditions promote floppy growth and shorten its life.

planting.note: Direct-sow into deep, dry sandy soil after the last frost, choosing an open, disturbed, or lean site.

directions: Direct-sow into deep, dry sandy soil after the last frost, choosing an open, disturbed, or lean site since this Texas native resents rich, moisture-retentive beds. Found naturally in sandy soils along the middle Texas Gulf Coast, the post oak belt, and the Rolling and High Plains, it produces thimble-shaped lavender-pink flowers with a distinctive dark red style from June through November. It is a strong late-season nectar source for bees, butterflies, and moths, and several butterfly and moth larvae use it as a host plant. Its extended bloom window makes it a valuable filler for a Gulf Coast dry-meadow planting once summer heat has stalled other wildflowers.

planting.note: Set divisions or plugs in spring into consistently damp to seasonally wet soil, letting trailing stems root along the ground.

directions: Set divisions or plugs in spring into consistently damp to seasonally wet soil, such as ditch banks, pond edges, or low spots that hold water after Gulf Coast rains, and let the trailing stems root along the ground to knit into a dense mat. Its tiny white-to-lavender flower clusters bloom nearly all season and are a favorite of bumblebees, sweat bees, small butterflies, and skippers, making it an excellent low-growing companion to taller wetland wildflowers. It spreads readily by rooting stems, so give it room or use it intentionally as an erosion-control groundcover in soggy sites unsuited to turfgrass. It tolerates occasional foot traffic and mowing once established.

planting.note: Direct-sow into well-drained, gravelly or sandy soil in spring, choosing a hot, dry site.

directions: Direct-sow into well-drained, gravelly or sandy soil in spring, choosing a hot, dry site since this compact Texas native thrives on neglect once established. It forms a tidy mound of gray-green foliage studded with small white, yellow-centered daisies for much of the growing season, drawing in native bees and small butterflies. Though it closely resembles the more widely grown blackfoot daisy, it is a genetically and morphologically distinct species concentrated in central and south-central Texas. Avoid overwatering or heavy soils, which quickly cause crown rot in this drought-adapted plant.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
